steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist, knuckles facing forward.
Raise the closed fist to the side of your chin, knuckles pointing outward.
Tap the knuckles against your chin twice, with two crisp beats.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your cheek throughout both taps.
Nod once as you finish, so it reads as a definite number.
tip: The same sign covers maths and mathematics — context tells them apart.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands, fingers pressed firmly together.
Press the palms together in front of your chest, fingertips pointing forward.
Swing both hands outward and apart twice, like opening a book's covers.
Keep your palms facing each other as the hands open and close.
Mouth the word 'book' silently while you sign, to fix the meaning.
tip: Think of two covers swinging open — the double motion names the object itself.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, zigzagging from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide over the page.
Fix your gaze on the moving fingertips, as if your eyes are reading along.
tip: The V's fingertips are 'eyes' scanning the lines — mime them reading each word.

steps: Open your dominant hand beside your head, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand just to the side of your temple, palm angled inward.
Draw the hand slightly backward while your fingers close together into a pinch.
Keep the motion small and close to the head, finishing with pinched fingertips.
Keep a thoughtful, attentive expression, as if an idea has just landed.
tip: One-handed at the temple is the most widely taught form; some regions use both hands moving toward the forehead instead.

steps: Curve both hands into full C shapes, thumbs opposing the fingertips.
Hold the two C hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart.
Tip the hands toward each other in alternating inward pouring motions.
Keep the pouring smooth and rhythmic, like decanting between two beakers.
Wear a curious, inquisitive expression — science is about wondering.
tip: Picture pouring liquid back and forth between two cupped beakers.

steps: Press both flat hands together in front of your chest, palms touching.
Open and close the hands repeatedly, like flicking through a book's pages.
Travel both hands sideways as they open and close, covering a short distance.
Keep your palms facing each other through every opening motion.
Glance along the path of the moving hands, as if scanning a shelf.
tip: The book sign repeated while moving sideways — a whole shelf of books.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright in front of your torso, fingers pointing forward.
Move the hand straight down once, in one clean stroke.
Keep the C handshape steady and the palm facing sideways through the drop.
Mouth the word 'student' silently, since the same sign also means person and pupil.
tip: One manual sign covers student, person and pupil — mouthing picks the English word.

steps: Close both hands into relaxed fists in front of your body.
Bring the fists together so the outer edges meet at chest height.
Tap the hands against each other twice, with two light, even beats.
Keep both palms facing inward and the wrists relaxed through the taps.
Keep the taps small and crisp — big swings start to look like clapping.
tip: Two light taps of fist on fist — the rhythm of stacking sheets of paper.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger into a small circle.
Spread your remaining fingers open behind the pinched thumb-and-index circle.
Hold the hand in front of your chest and draw a question mark in the air.
Trace the hook first, then dot it with a short downward flick.
Raise your eyebrows and lean slightly forward, the classic questioning face.
tip: You are literally drawing a '?' in the air — hook, then dot.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against your thumb, as if holding a pen.
Make small side-to-side scribbling motions across the open palm surface.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways and the strokes quick and light.
Keep the writing hand moving — a still pen on a palm reads as pointing.
tip: The same writing motion covers pen, pencil and scribble — the tool is in the handshape.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, tucking the other fingers away.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, fingers pointing upward.
Hold the hands briefly at temple height, framing your head.
Keep both palms facing each other across the sides of your head.
Mouth the word 'teacher' silently, since regional variants of this sign exist.
tip: Two index fingers raised like antennae at the head — mouthing fixes it as teacher.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C shape, thumb opposing the fingertips.
Hold the C hand in front of your chest, fingers pointing forward.
Rotate your wrist downward, sweeping the hand over as if marking each person.
Repeat the downward rotation two or three times, shifting slightly sideways.
Keep your expression open and inclusive — you are gathering a crowd.
tip: Several regional variants exist; this wrist-rotating version is among the most widely used.

steps: Pinch both thumbs against index fingers to form two F handshapes.
Hold both F hands in front of your body, a few inches apart.
Move the hands together in a small horizontal clockwise circle.
Keep the F circles intact and the motion smooth through the loop.
Soften your face with a warm expression — family is an affectionate sign.
tip: Two F hands circling like a family gathered around a table; some regions use an open hand instead.

steps: Open your dominant hand with the fingers together, thumb relaxed.
Place the open hand around your chin, fingertips near the jawline.
Slide the hand downward while fingers and thumb close together, tracing a beard.
Keep the palm angled toward your face through the downward slide.
Finish with the hand just below the chin, fingers lightly pinched.
tip: Traces a beard down the chin — the same sign also means male and masculine.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright before your torso, fingertips pointing forward.
Bring the hand straight down once, in a single smooth stroke.
Hold the C shape firm and the palm facing sideways during the drop.
Mouth the word 'person' silently, since the same sign also means student and pupil.
tip: One manual sign, three English words — mouthing selects person, student or pupil.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat and open, palm facing downward.
Raise the flat hand to about chest height in front of you.
Bob the hand down once, as if patting the top of a child's head.
Keep the palm facing down and the fingers together through the bob.
Smile gently — the sign carries the warmth of the pat itself.
tip: One pat means a child; repeat the bob while moving sideways and it becomes 'children'.

steps: Close your dominant hand, extending only the index finger upward.
Touch the fingertip to your cheek, just below the cheekbone.
Brush the finger downward along the cheek twice, with two light strokes.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your face through both strokes.
Mouth the word 'woman' silently — the same sign also covers girl and lady.
tip: One finger brushing the cheek twice; mouthing picks woman, girl or lady.
